uncited: Diffuse Lighting Models calculate the scattering of light from a surface, providing the primary cue for shape and depth in ray-marched volume rendering and SDF rendering.

Unlike specular models that highlight surface gloss or ambient models that provide uniform illumination, diffuse models compute light intensity based on the angle between the surface normal and the light direction.

This family is distinct from [Distance Color Blending](791-distance-color-blending.md) by integrating directional light vectors and from [Ray-marched Shadows](1087-ray-marched-shadows.md) by assuming unobstructed light paths unless combined with shadowing techniques.
All models in this family rely on the geometric relationship between the surface normal $\mathbf{N}$ and the light direction $\mathbf{L}$.
The core mechanism involves computing the dot product $\mathbf{N} \cdot \mathbf{L}$ to determine the projected area of the light source onto the surface.
This value is clamped to $[0, 1]$ to prevent back-face illumination and negative lighting contributions.
where $(\cdot)_+$ denotes the positive part (clamping negatives to zero), $C_{base}$ is the material albedo, and $C_{light}$ is the light color intensity.
Normals are derived either analytically from the SDF gradient or via finite differences in volume data.
The Lambertian model, named after Johann Heinrich Lambert, is the standard for ideal diffuse reflection.
In the context of volume rendering and SDFs, these models were adapted to work with implicit surfaces where normals are derived from gradients rather than mesh topology.
